messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arthur has spent fifty years as a journalist, documenting the fault lines of other people’s lives. At seventy-three, he believed he was fireproof, a professional observer insulated by his notepad and camera. That belief ended six months ago, on a clear Tuesday morning at the Sterling Chemical plant. He was there on assignment, ironically for a feature on new industrial safety standards. He remembers the low, guttural groan of the ground, a vibration that travelled up through the soles of his shoes just before the world erupted. The first explosion was a wave of pure force that threw him against a chain-link fence. In the chaotic aftermath, with alarms blaring and smoke blotting out the sun, his professional instincts took over. He raised his camera, framing a shot of a twisted metal gantry against the toxic orange sky. But it was the taste he would never forget—a thick, acrid, metallic dust that coated his tongue and the back of his throat, the flavour of burnt chemicals and pulverized concrete.

In the months that have followed, that moment is not a memory he recalls but an event he perpetually relives. The image he captured through his viewfinder plays on a loop in his mind, and with it comes the phantom taste, so vivid he sometimes gags, convinced the dust is still in his mouth. When he tries to recount the event, the story feels foreign, like a dramatic wire report he’s reading about someone else. The sheer scale of the chaos makes it hard to believe it actually happened to him; it feels more like a film he watched than a day he survived. This sense of unreality is a stark contrast to the hyper-real vigilance that now governs his life. In his quiet, solitary apartment, he finds he is unable to relax. He sits in the dark, listening for any sound that might signal an intrusion, his body coiled tight with an anticipation of threat that never subsides.

His world has shrunk dramatically. He used to love working from bustling coffee shops, but now the unpredictability of public spaces is unbearable. If he must meet someone, he will only take a seat against a wall, where he can see the entrance and every person in the room. Any sudden noise—a car backfiring, a dish clattering to the floor—can cause him to freeze completely, his muscles locking, his mind a white-hot blank for several seconds. His gaze, once trained to find the telling detail for a story, now automatically inventories every room for potential weapons: a heavy glass ashtray, a tightly rolled magazine, a letter opener on a desk. He has come to believe that the world is fundamentally unsafe and that another disaster is always imminent.

To manage the intrusive memories and constant anxiety, Arthur has developed habits that offer momentary relief but are costing him dearly. He actively avoids thinking about the explosion, certain that if he were to let the full force of the memory in, he would not be able to handle it. The feeling is one of being permanently broken, that he will never be able to feel normal emotions again. His long and storied career, once the bedrock of his identity, now feels pointless; nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore. In the lonely hours of the night, he scrolls through websites, buying things he doesn’t need—rare books, vintage camera lenses, expensive watches. The brief, predictable thrill of the transaction is a balm, a small pocket of control in a life that feels utterly chaotic. The credit card debt is piling up, a concrete consequence of his nightly ritual of avoidance. It was a call from his bank that finally prompted him to seek help. Arthur arrived at his first session not with any grand hope for recovery, but with a quiet, desperate fear that the man he was before the explosion is gone forever, another casualty buried in the chemical dust.
